chapter: Dance tastes, big bands and the boat
title: Arcadia Ballroom and the Balkan Age in New York
summary: DeDroit's Dixieland band was sent by Lopez's office to the Arcadia Ballroom near Ray Miller's band and then packed the Balkan Age at 66th and Columbus.

story.theme_name: Coming to New York: clubs, jams, and making it

blocks.x: So they sent us over to the Arcadia Ballroom and they had Ray Miller there, and he had Frank Trombauer, I guess if you heard of him, played a C melody saxophone. Mike, how you played it. He had the greatest musicians in that band. Well that was the featured band. So this fellow, Fagan, who ran the place, he wanted to hear us and we played. He says, boy I'd like to put you and this band on the baseball field and see who can play the loudest. We played as loud as this big band. But Dixon, man, we hit it. You know, I mean, we didn't lay back. If we took a soft course it was just part of the arrangement. And strange as it may seem, although we played without music, we played arrangements. In the head. I mean we tried to keep the good stuff. We couldn't remember that. No Dixon man remembers what he played yesterday. You know what I mean? It's always new and it comes out of your head. You know, you might find the licks reminiscent, but it's hard to, like when you say, write it down. You write it down and you play it, it sounds terrible. You know, it doesn't sound, it must be spontaneous. So Fagan says, you fellas are great. He says, when can you start? I said, I can't start. He says, well where did you come here from? I said, my agent sent me.

He went on at a rate. And he told the agent, don't send any band here, they can't take the job. And the man said, thought he had a prize. And he did. Because we filled that, there was two isle codes, you know, one would open and a big band and they'd open up and you know, it was done in an artistic style, but it was strictly a ballroom. And you know, it isn't like this. Because truthfully, I don't think there was anything there that played like us. Now the Memphis Five were very popular and they played very well. And the Wolverines were popular and played well. But they didn't play in New Orleans. You see what I mean?
They didn't play. They played true Dixieland.

Oh I see. They played with a beat and they had good men. I remember distinctly that one Sunday, we gave a Sunday matinee, and I had to play the matinee for which I got off on Monday night. The other band called themselves the Circle Quintet, and they were my friends supposedly, but I think they would like to take me down a notch or two, you see? So they brought Bix Spider back in there. Well I said, is that Bix Spider back? They said yes. I said, well I have nothing to worry about. And I went home. Because it wasn't Bix's fault. It was the accompaniment he was getting from that other band who knew nothing about Bix Spider back. But his own band was a star. And they used to make records very good. But it wasn't Dixie. Mm-hm. But it wasn't Dixie. Mm-hm. I was selling Dixie Land band. And when I played the first tune in the Balcanese the people went wild. in the Balkan Age, the people went wild. And you know what it was? Red Hot, mommy remember that? It had a beat. They said, that's the Balkan Age, and we packed that joint, and I had my name in the lights, and I never even took a picture of it. I didn't worry about it. I don't know what kind of a…
At 66th and Columbus. It's a continuation of Broadway. You know what Columbus cycle?
Well, I'm not familiar with it.

They had four places in that one building. Ours was the ballroom. We had Healy's Restaurant on the bottom floor. About that time, the Duke of Wales was cutting quite a sloth in New York. He was a ladies' man, and he used to go to Healy's, and maybe he helped us, I don't know. But it was a very popular spot, 66th and Columbus.
